title: We hardened our CI/CD pipeline in one day. Here's what broke first.
sub: Merging five pull requests on a private GCP shell.
problem: CI ran on private runners in GCP, but every change to those runners was risky.
Our own safety gate blocked any change that replaced a resource, even a harmless one.
did: Merged multi-language gates: Terraform/HCL, TypeScript, Python, Go
Turned on security alerts for IAM, key, firewall, bucket, and policy changes
Fixed runner boots: retries, unique names, safe rollouts
Gave the no-destroy gate a reviewed allow-list with an expiry
lesson: A safety gate with no exception path doesn't make you safe. It makes whole classes of change unshippable.

title: Four failures in one day. Not one was caught by an alert.
sub: Why every incident record now names the missing signal.
problem: Every failure that day was found by a person looking at a queue or a log.
The platform had no telemetry on its own CI.
did: A single GitHub API timeout failed a runner boot
A stale registration trapped a runner in a 409 loop
Cloud Monitoring rejected alert filters that passed plan
Near miss: a rollout would have deleted the VM running its own apply
lesson: A plan is not proof. If a person had to find it, the record must add the signal that would have found it.

title: The riskiest resource in our cloud was one nobody created.
sub: Narrowing access across CI, cloud, and people.
problem: GCP had auto-created a default network with SSH and RDP open to the whole internet.
Shared CI workflows and an admin login had more reach than they needed.
did: Shared CI workflows reachable only by the owner's repos, never public
Workflows default to read-only, with permissions granted per job
Flagged the default network for deletion
Removed an admin user's console password until SSO replaces it
lesson: Least privilege isn't a one-time setting. It's a habit of asking 'who can reach this?' every time.

title: CI checks stop bad pull requests. What stops everything else?
sub: Guardrails enforced by the cloud itself.
problem: Every check we had ran in CI.
A console click, a stolen credential, or a third-party agent could skip the pull request entirely.
did: Defined 13 GOV-* guardrails mapped to GCP org policies and AWS SCPs
Wrote one machine-readable baseline, validated by JSON Schema
Every control states what it guarantees and what it does not
Dry run first; every exception needs an owner, a reason, and an expiry
lesson: Governance comes before services. A service is fast to build when the guardrails already exist.

title: A security control you haven't tested is a hope.
sub: Why we count verified controls, not documented ones.
problem: A policy can look right and still not match how the cloud authorizes a request.
Our own alert filters passed review and plan, then failed at the API.
did: Four stages per control: specified, schema-validated, integration-tested, adversarially verified
Verified is not enforced: enforcement is observed live, never claimed in a file
Evidence must exist as a trace, a log line, and a metric
First milestone: prove 3 controls end to end in a disposable test folder
lesson: One verified control is worth more than ten documented ones.

title: How long should a cloud credential live? We picked a number.
sub: Session and credential lifetimes, grounded in NIST.
problem: 'Short-lived' meant nothing until it had a number.
Our AI builder was about to use an admin user's static keys.
did: Cloud credentials live 1 hour by default and at most
Re-authenticate within 24 h (NIST AAL2), 12 h for prod and admin (AAL3)
A new, empty AWS management account, because SCPs never apply to it
The AI builder reaches Bedrock only through SSO
lesson: Fifteen extra minutes of setup now beats a permanent gap in governance.

title: We fixed a bug. The same bug lived on in its copy.
sub: What a duplication review across five repos found.
problem: A retry fix landed in one startup script and missed the identical one next to it.
AI agents make this worse: without a map, they rewrite what already exists.
did: Scanned five repos for copy-pasted code
Found the same prompts copied four times, and only one copy is read
Moved shared contracts to one home, vendored everywhere
Wrote a rule of three: extract on the second copy for security and contracts
lesson: Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, but a duplicated security fix is a vulnerability.

title: An AI code reviewer that spends tokens only where code can't decide.
sub: Designing the review loop before writing it.
problem: A single big AI reviewer sees too much, costs too much, and loops forever.
Infrastructure failures were being sent to the AI to 'fix'.
did: Build fails: classify first, and only real code errors reach the AI builder
Build passes: deterministic gates, then the AI reviewer per unit
The model asks for evidence; code fetches it. At most 2 calls per unit
A cap of 4 review rounds, with 3 or fewer as the measured target
lesson: Tools hold capability, agents hold judgment. A tool never loops and never decides.

title: Pick the cheapest AI model that can handle the change.
sub: Routing by complexity, measured per function.
problem: Sending every change to a frontier model is expensive.
File-level complexity scores bury a risky change inside a big file.
did: The router answers questions about complexity, never about routing
Per-function cognitive complexity using Sonar's published rules
Checked against Sonar's own totals, so the numbers can't drift
Combined with blast radius: how many callers the changed code has
stats: model calls to pick a model
lesson: No model should ever run just to decide which model to run.

title: Measure your AI reviewer before you optimize it.
sub: A benchmark with ground truth, built from our own code.
problem: Every optimization claim ('70% cheaper') was a guess.
There was no baseline to compare against.
did: 104 frozen test cases from real files in TypeScript, Python, and Terraform
Seeded defects with known answers, plus clean changes
Compared full-file vs diff-only review through the real reviewer
A deterministic judge: no AI grading another AI
lesson: The first probe found 7 of 8 calls timing out on a laptop CPU. Hardware, not the model, set the result.

title: Free scanners caught half the bugs before any AI looked.
sub: Where an AI reviewer actually has to earn its cost.
problem: It's easy to credit an AI with catching bugs a free tool already catches.
The real question: what does the AI add?
did: Ran Checkov, Trivy, Gitleaks, Semgrep, and Bandit on the same cases
Scored findings by exact line, so old issues earn no credit
Every Terraform defect and hardcoded secret: caught by tools
Logged secrets, path traversal, dropped awaits, unbounded loops: missed by all
stats: of seeded defects caught by tools
lesson: Judge an AI reviewer only on what deterministic tools miss. Everywhere else it just adds cost.

title: A valid AI model test for about a dollar.
sub: Running a GPU benchmark on spot VMs, safely.
problem: A laptop CPU can't run the 7B model inside the reviewer's timeout.
GPU time is expensive if a VM is forgotten.
did: Checked live prices: a spot L4 GPU VM is $0.423/hour (us-central1)
One VM per run, created from a template with no standing cost
A time limit that Google Cloud itself enforces, so the VM deletes itself
The run aborts unless the model is confirmed in GPU memory
lesson: A silent CPU fallback must never pass as a GPU result. Guard the measurement, not just the bill.
